items.title: A Game About A Delivery Raccoon On A BMX Bike Is Making Me Nostalgic For My Childhood Summers
items.author: Rebekah Valentine
items.summary: I’ve recently found myself drawn to media portrayals of summer in rural Japan, of which there are many. I think I’m feeling a weird sort of half-nostalgia.
items.text:
I’ve recently found myself drawn to media portrayals of summer in rural Japan, of which there are many. I think I’m feeling a weird sort of half-nostalgia. I’ve never experienced a Japanese summer specifically. But we’re suffering from a dearth of games about American suburban summers, and games like Boku no Natsuyasumi, Shin-Chan: Me and the Professor on Summer Vacation, and Yo-Kai Watch portray childhood experiences that aren’t that far off from my own.

I used to spend summers at my grandmother’s house, running all over the neighborhood with my friends without adult interference through backyards, down to the creek, into the “woods” (really just a copse, but we were small!), through that one field with all the tall grass. We looked for cool rocks, climbed trees, ate popsicles, rode bikes in circles, and picked and ate mulberries. And there’s that cicada sound that’s always in such summer games, and the fireflies at night. Hell, the vibes are close enough that Tim Rogers did a whole six-hour video essay on Boku no Natsuyasumi and my own hometown.

I’m always on the lookout for more games that give me a little taste of that summer feeling, so I was drawn to a demo of upcoming indie Tanuki: Pon’s Summer at PAX West (there’s a free demo on Steam you can play now, too, if you like). Pon’s Summer is significantly different from any of my own summers: it stars a lazy raccoon working as a mail carrier in a rural town, trying to earn enough to restore a shrine before the end of summer, none of which I can relate to. But Pon does happen to own a sick bicycle. His is a BMX, unlike mine, but the way he rides it all over the little town and tries to do sick tricks with it is very familiar. The raccoon, oddly, is better than I was at popping wheelies, but I’m also about as bad at controlling him as I was at controlling my own bike. It’s funny. A little nostalgic!

Pon delivers the mail. He collects the packages each day and sorts them in his backpack, fitting the shapes together perfectly so he can carry them all at once. To uphold the dignity of the post office, Pon also helps with basically any odd job anyone wants him to do, and is encouraged to meander and goof off in between deliveries as long as they, eventually, get done. In the little scenarios I ran into with the townsfolk, that meant taking some photos for a creatively drained photographer and stopping by the local pub to help pour some brews. I have to tip the glass and get the foam pour exactly right to each patron’s specifications to please the barkeep. Add this to the growing list of activities I am humorously hopeless at.

I’m finding little to relate to personally here (for some reason no one let me pour beer as a child). Perhaps because this is a game about a raccoon more than about a human childhood experience. But I’m having fun. The raccoon is nice and round, so his activities on a BMX bike are inherently funny and seemingly also amusing to the all-human townsfolk. There are lots of little ramps and rails all over town to practice on, and some surprisingly difficult challenges strewn about such as riding through checkpoints as fast as possible or getting a certain trick score, a la Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater, within a certain amount of time.

And taken as a whole, Pon’s Summer encompasses one feeling I did love from those youthful summers: this sort of meandering, ordinary freedom. When you become an adult, you get a job and no summers off, and riding bikes becomes exercise instead of fun, and people don’t let you run through their backyards anymore (well, maybe they just don’t let anyone do that nowadays). I don’t think I’ve aimlessly wandered through my own neighborhood since I was a teenager, and I can’t imagine a real-life scenario when I’ll ever get to do that again. Pon’s Summer is a light, cute way to recapture that feeling, just for a bit. So even though he’s a lazy raccoon, there’s a part of me that longs to embody Pon for a summer again: fall down, scrape my knees, mess things up a bit without serious consequence, stop and listen to those cicadas.

items.title: Brutal Cult-Favorite Indie Survival Game Is Almost Free After Years Of Legal Limbo With Adult Swim’s Defunct Publishing Label
items.author: Rebekah Valentine
items.summary: In 2017’s Rain World, the slow and clumsy slug cat struggles out of its burrow and into the world. It cannot climb; it can barely jump. Food is scarce. Almost
items.text:
In 2017’s Rain World, the slow and clumsy slug cat struggles out of its burrow and into the world. It cannot climb; it can barely jump. Food is scarce. Almost everything its size and bigger is a predator that is faster and stronger than it, and will consume it without a thought. If it does not fill its belly and find shelter in time, deadly rains will kill it.

And yet, the slug cat persists. So too has Rain World.

I first fell in love with Rain World about five or six hours into trying to review it early in my career. What did it for me was watching an enemy pick up a stick I’d been muddling around with prior to spotting it, and yoink the stick across the map at me like a spear, pinning me to a wall. The enemy caught me, and I died. But on my next run, I found another stick, and was able to do the exact same thing myself, using the stick as a platform to climb to areas I hadn’t been able to reach before. The game never showed me how; my enemies did, silently and by accidents of their AI.

Rain World is such a wonderful, weirdo game, it’s not surprising to me that it took a long time to really find its audience. Years, even. Developer Videocult first launched it nine years ago, in 2017, with the now-essentially-defunct Adult Swim Games publishing it on PS4 and PC, and eventually porting it to Nintendo Switch. For quite a while, the state of Rain World was a messy one. Different platforms in different regions received inconsistent updates. At one point, the game was at version 1.5 on PC, 1.7 on consoles, and, inexplicably, 1.8 on PC in Korea. A promised Xbox edition had yet to manifest. There were bugs not getting patched effectively, and a lot of reasonably grouchy yet persistent fans.

In the midst of all this, Akupara Games CEO David Logan and head of publishing Buddy Sola were a newly-formed work-for-hire company looking for clients. They saw the state of Rain World, and, like a slug cat, pounced.

“From my perspective with Adult Swim, things were just sort of stagnant,” Logan says. “You know, they weren’t moving up. They weren’t moving down. They were sort of just, you know, the community was really maintaining the live ops for the game and maintaining, but it was like a small, low-burning flame. And we threw fuel on the fire and ignited the fire and made it really take off.”

Thus Akupara Games took over publishing for Rain World in 2022, after a lot of behind-the-scenes legal back-and-forth.Their first goal was to get all the versions of the game consistent with one another. But once that was done, they wanted to do more. When Akupara took the helm, Logan and Sola tell me, the all-time peak concurrent player count in Rain World was around 600. It was not a widely popular game, but it did have an extraordinarily devoted community that had stuck around through some rough times, which suggested to them that Rain World could be pushed farther. They leveraged that community for the game’s first DLC in 2023, Downpour, which was adapted from a popular mod. Their team began holding community events: art contests, live streams, ARGs. They sold physical merchandise. They released the game on Xbox at last. And the community responded to these things, far more strongly (say Logan and Sola) than communities for other games they had published.

Downpour brought the peak concurrent player count to 8,500. The second DLC, The Watcher, in 2025 got them to 15,500. Logan and Sola tell me the first DLC release sold 186,000 units, and the second sold 128,000 at their respective launches. Recently, during a single Steam summer sale, Rain World itself sold 1.3 million units on deep discount, and its sales since Akupara took over have reached 3.5 million total.

To me, this is nuts. Rain World is a really weird game. It’s harsh. It doesn’t explain itself much, but rather unfolds bit by bit as you play and observe. You die a lot, and lose progress, and restart, and get lost, and sometimes are put in unwinnable situations. Various updates over the years have offered easier playstyles and more tutorials, but at its core, Rain World is brutal and inscrutable. I express this surprise to Logan and Sola in our interview, and they admit that the median playtime on Rain World is pretty low. But those who do play actively are very invested, and they find their community has a surprisingly large population of individuals who don’t play at all themselves; they watch streamers instead, but still buy merchandise and show up in community spaces.

“We have now generated over seven figures in revenue just on merch alone, which is wild, because most of our games are doing, like, low thousands in merch,” Logan says. “And so, over seven figures was just phenomenal. And that’s what we’ve received as the revenue, so, I’m guessing it’s, like, even eight figures at this point.”

I spoke to Logan and Sola ahead of the game’s ninth anniversary livestream, during which Videocult and Akupara Games announced a shiny new physical collector’s edition for this nine-year-old sicko game that I would not have, in a million years, thought would get something like this when I first played it in 2017. But more interesting to me is what’s going on behind the scenes simultaneously: Logan and Sola tell me that despite Akupara owning the publishing rights and license, Rain World is still quietly tied to Adult Swim Games, or whatever remains of it after WB seemingly retired the label in 2024 (we’ve reached out to WB for comment). At the time, Adult Swim Games was under fire for its initial plan to simply delist all the games it still published, a move that would have created chaos and headache for developers. After an outcry, the company eventually returned publishing rights to a number of (not all) developers.

With that, it seems that WB is actively trying to offload any remaining obligations or ties left behind by what remains of the label, and that includes its remaining ties to Videocult and Rain World. The folks from Akupara wouldn’t get into specifics, but Logan says he thinks an end is in sight.

“Recently we’ve continued talking, and we hope we are close to a resolution with them,” he says. “That said, I also reached out to you a couple years [ago] with I think a similar story to this, and I thought we were close at that point as well, so we are hoping that we can be fully independent.”

Regardless of outcome, Rain World will continue, say Logan and Sola, in some fashion. Likely not in the form of more DLC. They tell me that Videocult has effectively pushed the game to its limits; it’s nine years old, they can only fit so much stuff in it. I asked after a Rain World 2, and Sola said, “That is not something that we are confirming.”

But something, to be sure. “We want to continue to do things, including games, including not games,” Logan says.

https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/blocks-for-babies-4.jpg

Rain World is such a wonderful, weirdo game, it’s not surprising to me that it took a long time to really find its audience. Years, even. Developer Videocult first launched it nine years ago, in 2017, with the now-essentially-defunct Adult Swim Games publishing it on PS4 and PC, and eventually porting it to Nintendo Switch. For quite a while, the state of Rain World was a messy one. Different platforms in different regions received inconsistent updates. At one point, the game was at version 1.5 on PC, 1.7 on consoles, and, inexplicably, 1.8 on PC in Korea. A promised Xbox edition had yet to manifest. There were bugs not getting patched effectively, and a lot of reasonably grouchy yet persistent fans.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/rebounder.jpg

In the midst of all this, Akupara Games CEO David Logan and head of publishing Buddy Sola were a newly-formed work-for-hire company looking for clients. They saw the state of Rain World, and, like a slug cat, pounced.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/fps-2000s-sprawl-zero.jpg

“From my perspective with Adult Swim, things were just sort of stagnant,” Logan says. “You know, they weren’t moving up. They weren’t moving down. They were sort of just, you know, the community was really maintaining the live ops for the game and maintaining, but it was like a small, low-burning flame. And we threw fuel on the fire and ignited the fire and made it really take off.”
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/Project-P.I.T.T-image-from-Steam-store-page-Froke.jpg
blocks.c: Project P.i.t.t Image From Steam Store Page Froke

blocks.x: Thus Akupara Games took over publishing for Rain World in 2022, after a lot of behind-the-scenes legal back-and-forth.Their first goal was to get all the versions of the game consistent with one another. But once that was done, they wanted to do more. When Akupara took the helm, Logan and Sola tell me, the all-time peak concurrent player count in Rain World was around 600. It was not a widely popular game, but it did have an extraordinarily devoted community that had stuck around through some rough times, which suggested to them that Rain World could be pushed farther. They leveraged that community for the game’s first DLC in 2023, Downpour, which was adapted from a popular mod. Their team began holding community events: art contests, live streams, ARGs. They sold physical merchandise. They released the game on Xbox at last. And the community responded to these things, far more strongly (say Logan and Sola) than communities for other games they had published.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/maneater2.jpg

Downpour brought the peak concurrent player count to 8,500. The second DLC, The Watcher, in 2025 got them to 15,500. Logan and Sola tell me the first DLC release sold 186,000 units, and the second sold 128,000 at their respective launches. Recently, during a single Steam summer sale, Rain World itself sold 1.3 million units on deep discount, and its sales since Akupara took over have reached 3.5 million total.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/robloxas-160x160.jpg
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/8bXdtpmYfKdkTKxbKBQCiX-1920-80-160x160.jpg

To me, this is nuts. Rain World is a really weird game. It’s harsh. It doesn’t explain itself much, but rather unfolds bit by bit as you play and observe. You die a lot, and lose progress, and restart, and get lost, and sometimes are put in unwinnable situations. Various updates over the years have offered easier playstyles and more tutorials, but at its core, Rain World is brutal and inscrutable. I express this surprise to Logan and Sola in our interview, and they admit that the median playtime on Rain World is pretty low. But those who do play actively are very invested, and they find their community has a surprisingly large population of individuals who don’t play at all themselves; they watch streamers instead, but still buy merchandise and show up in community spaces.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2024/01/72076e81f857ff16517d5e52981eeb9f-160x160.jpg

“We have now generated over seven figures in revenue just on merch alone, which is wild, because most of our games are doing, like, low thousands in merch,” Logan says. “And so, over seven figures was just phenomenal. And that’s what we’ve received as the revenue, so, I’m guessing it’s, like, even eight figures at this point.”
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/twitch-ai-stream-coach-160x160.jpg

I spoke to Logan and Sola ahead of the game’s ninth anniversary livestream, during which Videocult and Akupara Games announced a shiny new physical collector’s edition for this nine-year-old sicko game that I would not have, in a million years, thought would get something like this when I first played it in 2017. But more interesting to me is what’s going on behind the scenes simultaneously: Logan and Sola tell me that despite Akupara owning the publishing rights and license, Rain World is still quietly tied to Adult Swim Games, or whatever remains of it after WB seemingly retired the label in 2024 (we’ve reached out to WB for comment). At the time, Adult Swim Games was under fire for its initial plan to simply delist all the games it still published, a move that would have created chaos and headache for developers. After an outcry, the company eventually returned publishing rights to a number of (not all) developers.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/dawnwalkerbear-160x160.jpg

With that, it seems that WB is actively trying to offload any remaining obligations or ties left behind by what remains of the label, and that includes its remaining ties to Videocult and Rain World. The folks from Akupara wouldn’t get into specifics, but Logan says he thinks an end is in sight.
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/ponssummer-160x160.jpg

“Recently we’ve continued talking, and we hope we are close to a resolution with them,” he says. “That said, I also reached out to you a couple years [ago] with I think a similar story to this, and I thought we were close at that point as well, so we are hoping that we can be fully independent.”
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2025/12/maxresdefault-160x160.jpg

Regardless of outcome, Rain World will continue, say Logan and Sola, in some fashion. Likely not in the form of more DLC. They tell me that Videocult has effectively pushed the game to its limits; it’s nine years old, they can only fit so much stuff in it. I asked after a Rain World 2, and Sola said, “That is not something that we are confirming.”
https://kotaku.com/app/uploads/2026/09/rain-world-160x160.jpg
But something, to be sure. “We want to continue to do things, including games, including not games,” Logan says.

items.title: GTA 6 Fans Track Down Real-World Version Of The Nudist Resort, Then Try To Extort It
items.author: John Walker
items.summary: During that week of regularly released two-minute leaks from GTA 6 courtesy of Cyberleek, in addition to consistently stunning us with the levels of fidelity
items.text:
During that week of regularly released two-minute leaks from GTA 6 courtesy of Cyberleek, in addition to consistently stunning us with the levels of fidelity and intricacy in the upcoming game, one of the most astonishing revelations was the existence of a nudist park in the game. Player character Jason Duval was seen walking among a huge range of uncensored naked resort guests who all had their bits and bobs exposed to the elements. The crypto-scamming leaker had Jason pull out binoculars to zoom in on body parts, and then ended the clip by attacking the nudists. Now, rather demoralizingly, unhinged GTA fans have managed to track down the Florida location on which the in-game resort is based and, according to GamesRadar, driven its owner to distraction. In fact, the nudist resort is claiming some reviews are attempting to blackmail the vacation spot.

Unhealthily obsessed investigators claim the real-world version of Grand Theft Auto VI‘s nudist resort is called Cypress Cove, located in Kissimmee, Florida. The resort offers a 9-hole golf course, tennis courts, and kayaking, with a day perhaps ending with a meal at the Cheeks Bar & Grill, and based on reviews on sites like Trip Advisor, it seems to be a very popular and well-liked place to visit. However, looking through reviews on Google sadly reveals a more confusing picture, as hilarious japesters have been posting reference after reference to GTA 6 and Jason Duval, causing the Cypress Cove owners to have to post responses trying to explain to real customers what is going on. And they aren’t happy.

Naked extortion

The issue is, instead of just giving the place a gag 5-star review and making some knowing reference, what people are doing is making reference to an “incident” taking place, many mentioning a man wandering on-site and using binoculars to spy on residents. And if you’re running a nudist business, that’s not a funny joke to see appearing in public reviews of your resort.

So it is that Cypress Cove has written a furious response to at least one of these reviews, while trying to play whack-a-mole with the dozens of others that keep popping up. In it, there are some very good-natured GTA 6 references (“We appreciate the commitment to the GTA storyline, but Cypress Cove is located in Florida—not Leonida,”), but also the very serious claim that some folks posting reviews have said the resort must pay them money to have them removed. At the time of writing, no reviews containing these threats remain, as it seems Cypress Cove has been pretty effective at getting Google to take them down. And a good job too, as the Cove remarks, “Unfortunately, our marketing budget also does not contain a line item for ‘internet ransom.'”

The full reply from Cypress Cove reads:

🚨 ⚠️ SPAM / EXTORTION REVIEW ⚠️ 🚨

❌ THIS IS NOT A LEGITIMATE GUEST REVIEW.

For anyone wondering about the suddenly recurring references to “Jason Duval,” “Lucia,” binoculars, a pool, firearms, and other suspiciously similar details — those are references to Grand Theft Auto VI. 🎮

Yes. A video game.

These reviews appear to be part of a coordinated series of fabricated posts using GTA VI references and attaching them to our actual business. They were then followed by a request that we PAY MONEY to have the reviews changed or removed.

💰 We will not pay.
🚫 We will not negotiate.
📸 We have documented the reviews and the request for payment.
📢 This activity is being reported through the appropriate channels. For our actual guests and anyone researching Cypress Cove: please understand that these posts do not describe genuine guest experiences at our resort.

And to whoever is behind them:

🎮 We appreciate the commitment to the GTA storyline, but Cypress Cove is located in Florida — not Leonida.

✨ Unfortunately, our marketing budget also does not contain a line item for “internet ransom.” ✨

🚫💵 NO PAYMENT. NO NEGOTIATION. FALSE REVIEW REPORTED.

items.title: PlayStation Reportedly Dropped Kojima’s Game Due To A Growing Budget And Missed Deadlines
items.author: Zack Zwiezen
items.summary: Earlier this week, PlayStation announced it was no longer going to publish Hideo Kojima’s Physint. At the time, it wasn’t clear why Sony was ditching Kojima,
items.text:
Earlier this week, PlayStation announced it was no longer going to publish Hideo Kojima’s Physint. At the time, it wasn’t clear why Sony was ditching Kojima, but a new report from Bloomberg explains that the project’s budget was growing too large and the team was missing deadlines which, along with other factors, led to PlayStation backing out, which in turn let Xbox swoop in to fund and publish the upcoming title.

On September 11, Bloomberg reported that, according to people familiar with the project, one major reason Sony cut ties with Physint was due to the commercial performance of Death Stranding and its sequel. These games reportedly didn’t meet PlayStation’s revenue expectations. Another issue is that Physint has reportedly missed deadlines and was on course to be overbudget. The game is reportedly still years away from completion, too, making Physint a very expensive investment for Sony. Another factor: PlayStation wasn’t excited to invest hundreds of millions of dollars into another game that, like Death Stranding, wouldn’t remain a PlayStation exclusive.

For many, the news was surprising. Kojima and PlayStation have had a long relationship, with the Metal Gear Solid franchise calling the console its main home for decades. And when Kojima and MGS publisher Konami parted ways in a messy, public split in 2015, it was PlayStation that swooped in to provide the famous game designer with funding for his next game, which would end up being Death Stranding. But Bloomberg reports that many of the PlayStation executives who had developed a close relationship with Kojima over the years are no longer at the company. Seemingly, those who remain don’t see investing in Kojima’s next big game as a valuable move.

Meanwhile, the outlet reports that Xbox and its new CEO, Asha Sharma, saw Physint as a good investment for a few reasons.

One of the main factors is the PC. Sony is reportedly done releasing PC ports of its big games (at least those that aren’t focused on online multiplayer), so the company wouldn’t make any money from the eventual release of Physint on PC via a different publisher. But Xbox releases all of its games on PC and reportedly is planning to do the same with Physint. The Xbox deal with Kojima also includes film and TV rights for both Physint and Kojima’s other current project, the horror game OD. That title was already being published by Xbox as part of an earlier deal.

“Betting on Kojima-san is an easy call,” an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg. “We believe in his team’s ability to build AAA games with groundbreaking, new IP and we believe in OD, Physint, and our growing partnership.”

For PlayStation, the timing of this news couldn’t be worse. The company is dealing with a lot of messy situations that have fans turning on them. The company’s recent announcement that it was ending physical game production in 2028 sparked a backlash that is still ongoing in the comments below every official PlayStation post. Wolverine, PlayStation’s next big exclusive game, has been getting middling reviews from critics. PlayStation has also suffered a number of high-profile misfires and cancellations as it continues to try to build live-service hits, but releases games like the short-lived Concord. Its treatment of Bungie and Destiny 2 has also angered many fans, as has its closing of studios like Bluepoint. So ditching Kojima’s next game, believed to be a Metal Gear-like stealth action game, is only going to be yet more bad news to dump on the pile.

items.title: Wardogs presents a different kind of FPS power fantasy: making fat stacks as a pacifist rideshare driver
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer
items.text:
Because no-one entirely likes their job, I should be upfront about my issues with newly launched Early Access darling Wardogs, the mass-scale multiplayer shooter in which I’ve just found employment. Its "Play like to you used to" tagline and Halo 3-aping trailer smell a bit of reactionary, stuck-in-the-past thinking. It’s a mass-scale multiplayer shooter, so individual heroics rarely influence match outcomes. And, like pretty much everyone else who sucked down both those problems and tried playing on launch night regardless, I spent far too long attempting to communicate with server architecture that clearly had the resilience of overmilked cornflakes.

And yet, the fifty minutes I did spend in a functioning match felt like some of the most pleasant and productive time I’ve had in a competitive FPS for ages. The secret: ignore all first person shooting entirely, and begin a lucrative career as an Uber driver for commuting mercs.

In a stark break from reality, Wardogs’ gig economy can be very profitable indeed. Almost every positive action earns you cash, from the obvious hardpoint captures and squadmate revives to the humble delivery of people and bandages to the frontlines. And, since team spawns are literal miles from the central battlezones, logistical roles are not merely cash-incentivised, but essential.

In an accurate reflection of reality, you begin with little, must buy all vehicles and equipment yourself, and are on the hook if they’re lost while on duty. But the creation of genuine rear-detachment roles means Wardogs solves problems I have with both big shooters, and the extraction subgenre it also borrows from: by constantly ferrying teammates, I can have an individual yet materially important impact on the match, and by never intentionally joining a gunfight, I need never worry about loot loss anxiety. It was the perfect career move.

Buoyed by first-day enthusiasm, once I finally loaded into a game I bought a car, directed it dutifully towards the crowd of pedestrian soldiers, and immediately caused a helicopter crash. My pull-up-to-the-kerb manoeuvre had unwittingly put me in the landing path of a descending attack chopper – a major fault in the standard United Kingdom driving test – forcing the delicate warbird to flip over my roof and explode. Its occupants, miraculously unhurt but quite cross, shot me a damning glance as they strode off to buy another one.

The rest of my inaugural fare, a full house of one real-life friend and two silent randomers, went mercifully smoother. Despite the slippery handling of my entry-level SUV, it was a comfortable, peaceful drive towards the hot zone, which itself offered ample parking space for my passengers to hop out. The prizes came instantly: $1,000 for a "tactical deployment", plus $500 for each of my unharmed passengers, plus a $15 tip from a particularly satisfied rider. $2,515 for a few kilometres of relaxed cruising? The hell am I doing as a deputy ed?

The private hire lifestyle took hold. For multiple runs, I’d steer back to base, wait next to other transit vehicles (sometimes sharing an “A’ight, mate” with the heli pilot next to me), load up on balaclava men, and deliver them vaguely near the sound of gunfire, my balance swelling with each trip. Half an hour in, I’d accumulated slightly higher earnings than my IRL friend, who’d been running around murdering people and getting shot himself. Sounds painful. Sounds like participating directly in the horrors of war, mankind’s most terrible creation, and a blight on the Earth that continues to destroy families and erase cultures every day. Sounds like he’s not even getting paid that much to do it anyway, the rube.

Meanwhile, my hands were clean, not counting all the filthy lucre that was crossing it. Granted, my usefulness was starting and ending with the thunk of automobile doors – sometimes I’d watch my disembarked comrades perish just moments after paying their fare, a tragically premature "Passenger survived, +$500" lingering onscreen as their heaped form shrunk in my rearview. In these moments I was less Iqbal, the friendly Prius owner who got me home from the pub last week, and more Charon, damned soul ferryman of the River Styx.

As the match went on, I also began having trouble with that key component of hypercapitalism: competition. It turned out those heli pilots were not my mates at all, but were conspiring to steal my business, adopting the unfair and likely illegal practice of having faster vehicles than me. Eventually, my stream of human tip jars reduced to a trickle of stragglers, the larger crowds routinely making a beeline for the nimbler, more spectacular choppers.

In search of alternative revenue streams, I diversified into supply logistics. At this point I hadn’t made quite enough profit to afford a proper truck, so instead bought one empty crate, chucked a few cheap medical supplies into it, and bunged it my car's back seat. Seemingly in ignorance of the massive boot, but whatever. I knew delivering it somewhere useful would require driving deeper into the fray than my people-carrying had thus far, but shareholder value (mine) demanded it.

The journey was, again, uneventful, and I chanced upon a makeshift base swarming with more action-inclined teammates. Surely, the kind of folk who’d appreciate a box of plasters. Not entirely familiar with the controls, I hit the G key to unload, at which point the create seemed to disappear. A "Supplies delivered, +$500" popped up – which, as my accountant tells me, if half what I could have made by filling those seats with bums instead – but I remained concerned about the supplies themselves. Beginning my search, I reversed, directly onto and over the bandage box that has been laying just out of view. Now, I was stuck, the car’s back end suspended barely high enough for the rear-wheel-drive wheels to regain purchase on the tarmac.

This was not ideal. As I got back at the wheel and tried wriggling free with Game Physics sorcery, I noticed the allies I’d come to resupply were no longer dashing around on the roof. Within seconds, a lone, green-dressed man with no 'Don’t shoot this one' arrow above his head rounded the building’s corner, rifle raised. Still stuck, I killed the engine and did the best impression of an empty, slightly slanted car that I’ll ever have to do. The man’s scope swivelled in my direction, then kept going, the ruse successful long enough for an arrowed teammate to pop out from behind a van and shoot him down.

Its "Play like to you used to" tagline and Halo 3-aping trailer smell a bit of reactionary, stuck-in-the-past thinking. It’s a mass-scale multiplayer shooter, so individual heroics rarely influence match outcomes. And, like pretty much everyone else who sucked down both those problems and tried playing on launch night regardless, I spent far too long attempting to communicate with server architecture that clearly had the resilience of overmilked cornflakes.

And yet, the fifty minutes I did spend in a functioning match felt like some of the most pleasant and productive time I’ve had in a competitive FPS for ages. The secret: ignore all first person shooting entirely, and begin a lucrative career as an Uber driver for commuting mercs.

In a stark break from reality, Wardogs’ gig economy can be very profitable indeed. And, since team spawns are literal miles from the central battlezones, logistical roles are not merely cash-incentivised, but essential.

It was the perfect career move.

Sounds like he’s not even getting paid that much to do it anyway, the rube.

items.title: Stylised XCOM-like tactics game Ex Sanguis straps Othercide's obsession with timelines to a leaner roguelike campaign
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute
items.text:
The nasal greenhorn strategy gamer understands "strategy" to be about mastery of space by means of clanging offensives, shining shieldwalls, and brute attrition, but the true Napoleon of Drag-Select knows that strategy is always, primarily, the mastery of time. I don't think Napoleon would have approved of Ex Sanguis. He would not have liked all the willowy clone women made out of congealed blood and pincers. He would have suspected them of being divorcees and Babouvists. But perhaps he would have appreciated the game's fixation with seizing the initiative.

As with Lightbulb's previous grid-based tactics RPG Othercide, Ex Sanguis has you going up against dozens of vaguely eschatological bladespawn with just the three austere and menacing bladegirls. There are generally a half-dozen foes to start with, and reinforcements soon hatch from gross eggsacs around the map. You can't simply overwhelm your opponents, then. Instead, you must pre-empt and interrupt them, anticipating their advance and dancing your best moves in first on the game's fluctuating timeline.

Some abilities are performed instantly, while others trigger after a delay. However initially inconvenient, the delays soon become an asset, as you learn to aim your artillery strikes where you know your enemies will be, a few score ticks from now. Other abilities trigger when an opponent acts, cutting them off. Or when a friendly deals some damage, adding a follow-up attack. A key question is whether to exhaust your regular action points and dip into your Burst bar, which lets you sneak in some extra licks at the cost of wildly postponing the character's next turn.

Watch on YouTube

And then there's repositioning: you get shoves, gravity pulses, and driving kicks that punt opponents around. This allows you to knock delayed enemy attacks off target, perhaps slamming the noxious seraphim into a boulder, or nudging them into the path of the AOE move you've just queued up with the previous character. As you preview these gambits, the character portraits and action indicators shuffle to and fro on the timeline. On higher difficulties, it's vitally important to avoid a scenario where the whole opposing force can take a turn, one after the other.

When I played Othercide, I didn't quite clock how much Lightbulb's approach has in common with Into The Breach. The resemblance feels a bit more prominent in Ex Sanguis. There's no fixed match countdown, true, but you're encouraged to finish fast: the angelbeasts are only going to get more numerous, and you generally aren't required to slaughter all of them - just a surgeon's handful of VIPs or a single enemy map fixture, sulking to the rear.

It's a messier experience than you'll find in Subset's game, however. The environments are full of blood blisters that blow up when struck, launching nearby characters a few squares. On more crowded maps, a single volatile pustule often triggers a prolonged cascade. The AI in the early access build seems overfond of setting the blisters off, in addition to controlling terrain. Some times, it's hellbent on swarming you; at others, it tries to lock down big portions of the map by preparing a delayed AOE move, wherever it finds itself.

The greater emphasis on terrain damage is one thing that distinguishes the early access version of Ex Sanguis from what I remember of Othercide. The other, more obvious point of departure is that Ex Sanguis has a trimmer roguelike structure, with more focussed progression.

On which note, here's my best effort at explaining the story: some kind of pesky vampire moon has leeched away the world's vital fluids and memories, reducing all of Creation to an ivory placeholder. You are the Mater, a goddess replete with the simmering intensity of Derek Zoolander. She can spawn duplicates of herself to fight the moon's minions. So far, it's very much the previous game's gothic mommy monster mash on fast-forward – all pout and glare and cod Latin metaphors, without much coherence but with a lot of enjoyable attitude.

It feels faster partly because there's less going on outside battle. Each run kicks you off with three warriors, allowing you to pick their classes – the initial options are broadly Swordlady, Gunlass and Time Wizardress - and starting abilities. You then trek across a cratered world map, fighting battles (with unlockable higher difficulties) and accumulating Corrupted Blood for campaign progression. Every battle you win nets you a choice of three further abilities or stat boosts per character.

Yes, we are operating in the realm of Vampire Survivors, just a teeny bit. As in the previous game and many other roguelikes, abilities form complementary sets, which are fun to unearth: for example, Swordlady can inflict bleed with one kind of melee attack, then slurp up the debuff to restore her own health. Eventually, you swill down enough Corrupted Blood from victories to access a bossfight, which functions as a chapter break. It's wise, of course, to pootle around a bit first, levelling up your murderdames and spending a bit of your Corrupted Blood on smaller lore discoveries that come with bonus abilities. When a run is over, whether due to beating a boss or defeat, you'll spend various flavours of ethereal substance on meta-unlocks that give you more things to unlock within runs.

I'm mixed on the new campaign format. I do miss the grottier, denser storytelling of the previous game, which grounded its stark monochrome abstractions in a narrative of obscure medieval abuses: it was like a neo-noir penny dreadful. I also took ghoulish pleasure in the ability to melt down your clone-daughters into primordial soup, treating the weaker ones as health packs for their more accomplished sisters, rather than just levelling everybody up. It's possible there are similarly revolting ideas at play later in Ex Sanguis.

Beyond that, I do wonder how much the new game's battle system and ability design really improves on Othercide's. I haven't yet discovered a blend of reaction and delayed abilities that really captivates me, in terms of how it lets me mess with the timeline and disrupt the horde.

Still, it's early days – I've only played three hours, and Ex Sanguis will spend at least six months in early access. If you really loved Othercide, I don't think there's anything here that will hugely disappoint you, just yet. You can read more about the game on Steam. Belated clarification: you do not have to be Napoleon or any other celebrated general to have opinions about Ex Sanguis. I'm not sure how Napoleon found his way into my intro, honestly.

items.title: Skyrim’s official IKEA crossover mod might be the most deftly-assembled Elder Scrolls gag ever, if not an ad blueprint other corps should follow
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim
items.text:
I didn’t think, when I saw the other day that Swedish furniture sellers IKEA had commissioned a group of modders to stick an advert for their wares in Skyrim as an official Bethesda-approved Creation, that I’d now be sitting here noting that I dug said creation’s dungeon designs.

I am, though, because I think that sums up the entire experience of playing through Kallax Storageborn. If all you do is read a headline about it or scan through the premise with a smirk, you might assume it’s just a soulless corporate stunt aiming to play off The Elder Scrolls 5’s well-established viral memeality, but without any depth that makes it worth dedicating the time to check out. That was largely how I felt about it too, up until I learned that highly skilled Fallout 4 Sim Settlements makers Kinggath Creations were the modders behind the free creation, and decided to check their work out for myself.

The secondary motivation I had for doing so was that in-game advertising feels like it’s being floated more often than ever at the moment as a way games might help pay for themselves, as the squeeze is felt across an industry desperate for maximum financial returns. Fantasy RPGs like Skyrim are arguably among the toughest places to naturally fit such ads, especially compared to the likes of sports games or James Bond adventures with special watches.

In terms of how it fits in Tamriel, you’ll probably be glad to learn that outside of loosely meshing with Skyrim’s established mechanics, Kallax Storageborn isn’t trying too hard to pretend that its additions are in any way lore-friendly. The first time you’re overencumbered after grabbing the mod, your character is sent a magical talking telegram informing them that a solution to their storage woes can be found in a dungeon called Storereach. Yep, that’s the tone set then.

Storereach starts off as a regular Skyrim cave, but grows into a well-made Dwarven dungeon assembled mostly from recognisable vanilla building blocks. Things really kick into gear when you reach the second level, Storereach Workshop. Here, the standard swells of Skyrim’s orchestral soundtrack morph into the quiet, but unmistakable jingle of distant elevator music as you wander into a Dwarven department store. In case you’re unsure, an apparition materialises to welcome you. If you’re anything like me, you’re completely distracted by the fact that next to him are specially made Dwarven versions of IKEA’s flatbed shopping trollies.

From there, you negotiate a maze of dioramas showing off Dwarven furnishings for different rooms, some of which have buttons you can press to trigger a short demonstration by ghostly salespeople. You learn about Stenrygg seats, Tavan rugs, and Gruskok kitchen sets. The place isn’t just an empty show hall, though: there’s some unique gear and a couple of secrets that are easily missed if you don’t peek around as many corners as you might in a standard dungeon delve. While some of the gags - such as a shield with a deflection enchantment dubbed the ‘Shield of the Returns Policy’ - are rather groan-worthy, a couple properly tickled me. For instance, I stumbled across a skeleton in the loos, bearing a note indicating they’d died after simply getting lost among the labyrinthine halls of the shop. That’s the sort of joke people make about going to IKEA, rather than one the retailers themselves would necessarily make, since it suggests their signage is a bit crap. It’s the sort of touch that stops the creation feeling too reverent or robotic in its efforts to convince you to buy a flat-pack bookcase called Billy, even when it’s giving you a spell that fires the retailer’s famous Swedish meatballs.

The mod’s main draw and namesake awaits in a chamber behind the store. Armed with a tome perfectly mimicking an IKEA instruction manual, and a staff shaped like an allen key, you assemble Kallax. Once its shelves have been inserted, this unit springs to life and starts speaking in comedian Matt Berry’s dulcet tones. He’s a new follower who’ll scrape along the ground behind you as you adventure and carry all of your burdens, much like a certain base game lady whose name rhymes with an STD. Cool. This is about where I expected the adventure to end, once I’d taken one more wander around Storereach to make sure I’d maxed out a loot haul that’s very potent if you rock up at a low level fresh out of Helgen. I can confirm that because I had to start over to try the IKEA mod, as a result of still not having gotten around to making sure my mod load order’s been updated to match last month’s new patch.

Alas, my adventure with Kallax was only beginning. After I’d crafted him his own version of Skyrim’s iconic iron helmet, he had me off to two more dungeons in search first of heirlooms from his missing master, and then in search of an assistant who might be able to shed light on his reason for existence. Along the way, I grew to love not so much Berry’s array of unique lines responding to places I visited and hijinks I got up to, but the more subtly hilarious touch of his footsteps constantly resembling the low rumble of wooden furniture being dragged along stone roads and through grassy undergrowth.

Eventually, we cornered the assistant in an ancient Nordic ruin chock full of clutter that you can order Kallax to clean up in order to unblock passages. I won’t spoil the ending, but I will note that the final chamber’s utterly majestic, and that along the way you’ll encounter the last few long-running Skyrim jokes the mod’s yet to hit. Many who’re sick of such gags and have low tolerance for any form of advertising will understandably roll their eyes so many times they end up unable to stop looking at the inside of their own heads.

I found it creative, well-crafted, and self-aware enough not to grate on me. I’m not even much of a Matt Berry fan either, which I think speaks to the job Kinggath and co have done of taking what could have been a licence to phone it in and trying just as hard as they would with a non-ad project. Even if they did miss out one key item from their Dwemer emporium. Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

Eventually, we cornered the assistant in an ancient Nordic ruin chock full of clutter that you can order Kallax to clean up in order to unblock passages. I won’t spoil the ending, but I will note that the final chamber’s utterly majestic, and that along the way you’ll encounter the last few long-running Skyrim jokes the mod’s yet to hit. Many who’re sick of such gags and have low tolerance for any form of advertising will understandably roll their eyes so many times they end up unable to stop looking at the inside of their own heads.

I found it creative, well-crafted, and self-aware enough not to grate on me. I’m not even much of a Matt Berry fan either, which I think speaks to the job Kinggath and co have done of taking what could have been a licence to phone it in and trying just as hard as they would with a non-ad project. Even if they did miss out one key item from their Dwemer emporium. Without having to lean on the mad Daedric prince Sheogorath - the ever-present crutch of any Elder Scrolls wackiness which threatens to tap on the fourth wall - they’ve created an officially rubber-stamped gag that’s worth more than five minutes of a player’s time.

That said, I don’t think Kallax Storageborn should necessarily serve as an example any corps or developers should look at when trying to insert their own palatable ads into Skyrim or any other game. The line it walks between endearing - if nakedly corporate - charm and off-putting cringe is very thin, and successfully negotiating it relies heavily on the unique blend of British and Scandinavian humour at play. If it were, say, an advert for a more American brand like Monster Energy or Little Caesars, I think it’d feel a lot more in-your-face and forced. Due to its meme-filled reputation, in large part built on the back of unofficial joke mods, Skyrim also suits this sort of tongue-in-cheek salespersonship a lot more easily than other RPGs. It’s an exception to the rule, rather than an ideal test case.

So, leave the neatly stored memories of captivating, if not overly lengthy, dungeons alone please. This shelving unit came together well, but it shouldn’t inspire legions to believe they can assemble an entire floor’s worth of bookcases without ending up with at least one screw out of place.

items.title: “Marvel’s Wolverine” is a Bloody Good Time, Bub
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s
items.text:
Superheroes really are back in 2026. As if they ever left. The record-breaking success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” segues nicely into next week’s long-awaited release of Insomniac’s “Marvel’s Wolverine,” a game with structural echoes of the company’s beloved “Spider-Man” games, with significantly less kid-friendly violence and more linear, intense storytelling. After a prologue/tutorial that feels a bit rocky in storytelling and gameplay, “Wolverine” settles in spectacularly, strapping players into a rollercoaster narrative and telling them not to panic. With remarkably fluid combat, gorgeous graphics, strong voice work, and compelling storytelling, this is one of the best games of 2026, which has already been a remarkably great year for gaming before roughly a dozen more intriguing titles come out before Thanksgiving. The Sony disc drama aside, it’s a good time to be a gamer.

“Marvel’s Wolverine” also owes a wonderful amount to the movies most readers have probably seen about the man with Adamantium bones. At first, it feels like it’s intentionally echoing the excellent “Logan,” the best film about this beloved character, in its sketch of a slightly older Wolverine forced into a protective role for more vulnerable mutants when the evil Bolivar Trask starts kidnapping them. The plan to eradicate mutantkind sends Logan back to his allies at Team X, including founder Nathaniel Essex and familiar faces like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Jean Grey, sketched very differently here than the Sadie Sink version from “BND.” More on that later.

After Team X rescues a group of mutants from Trask’s captivity, including Callisto, “Marvel’s Wolverine” pivots again to incorporate other comic book and film source material. It’s the kind of story that never directly mimics something you’ve seen before, but one can definitely feel the influence of Bryan Singer’s films on Logan’s search for identity and even Jean Grey’s ultimate arc (don’t worry, comic fans—I didn’t just spoil that it goes full Dark Phoenix à la the horrendous “The Last Stand”). As the story moves to Japan, it also brings in some of that country’s influence on this character, as seen cinematically in James Mangold’s underrated “The Wolverine.” You’ll even get to slice and dice your way through hundreds of members of The Hand, also seen in the best action sequence in “Brand New Day.”

And I do mean slice and dice. Parents should be warned that this game is far more violent than they may expect from the developers of “Miles Morales.” The developers don’t dull Logan’s blades in the slightest, allowing you to use them to stab, mutilate, and decapitate on a regular basis. The combat gameplay is familiar in its mix of strike, parry, dodge, and special powers, but it’s as fluid as any game like this that’s ever been released. As techniques, unlike new skills that recharge over time and one improves at the base mechanics, Wolverine becomes almost a Tasmanian Devil of a killing machine, taking enemies out at a rate befitting one of comicdom’s most beloved heroes. It gets to the point where one sees a dozen enemies and doesn’t question how to get through them but wonders why there aren’t more. By the time I got into my New Game Plus playthrough, I had fully mastered the combat of “Wolverine” as much as any game in years, and the adrenaline rush of a perfectly executed move simply never abates. I’ll honestly miss it.

Of course, a game can’t just be about decapitating fools who underestimated a man with claws. As for the rest of the experience, the set pieces are so spectacular that you can forgive the lackluster exploration. As for the latter, Logan often has to find something in a room to push the story forward, which basically just amounts to looking for the white dot that cues you to hit triangle. It’s not exactly thrilling. On the other hand, there are a couple of motorcycle set pieces that are so spectacular that you’ll wish there were more of them, and the big action sequences are as impressive as any MCU movie. The truth is that “Marvel’s Wolverine” gets the big and basic things right; so the minor connective tissue like running around the Team X facility to find the triangle that will push the story forward isn’t really a drag as much as a little break from the intensity before it becomes numbing.

Something else that elevates “Marvel’s Wolverine” over many games of this generation is its attention to environment. As you can imagine, when Logan turns into a blade whirlwind, nothing is safe, and the designers brilliantly allow you to leave a mark, whether it’s just a blade scratch on metal or something more intense. For example, you get into a fight in an arcade in Japan, and no claw machine is safe. Most combat sequences end in the kind of environmental destruction rarely seen in games where you can still take cover behind a wooden box, and it’s the kind of detail that really elevates the overall experience. It should also be noted that this game makes use of the PS5 controller in expansive ways, whether it’s a radio signal or just the hum and buzz of action. And the load times are insanely fast. You can go from startup to combat in actual seconds.

Finally, while “Marvel’s Wolverine” is incredibly fun, it’s also narratively richer than many superhero games. Without spoiling, Logan and Jean Grey become allies not just in stopping the big bad of this game but in figuring out the details of Logan’s lost past. Like in the Singer movies and some of the comic arcs, Logan is a killing machine who doesn’t really know how he got that way, and the script here lands in a place that’s both satisfying and poignant. It’s as rich as the great Uncanny X-Men arcs that this comic book fan grew up loving, and a reminder of how both superhero fiction and gaming can be so much more satisfying when it’s developed with true love, care, and mutilations.

Sony provided a review copy of this game. It is available on September 15, exclusively on PlayStation.

items.title: Bargain with demons and boat with the dead in joyful RPG heist quest anthology Thousand Hells
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the
items.text:
You'd expect a game called Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists to be on the depressing side, but this choose-your-own-adventure RPG anthology from the designers of King of Dragon Pass is an absolute tonic. It's a witty procession of Orphic descents, in which you assemble a crew of four garrulous weirdos and pitch them against quest scenarios that might involve talking trees, holy riddlers, and conduits of boiling blood.

There's an infectious, venturesome lightness to the game, which somehow persists alongside dire blunders and supernatural calamities that may see members of your party being cursed, punctured or unhinged. I've only completed a couple of the 10 heists across two hours of play, which makes me reluctant to call this an official review, but it's got my provisional recommendation. Come, reader - get thee to Pandemonium apace.

Watch on YouTube

Thousand Hells doesn't harbour a thousand distinct hells; its variety comes, instead, from choice of party members and the canny reshuffling of story beats, which play out against handsome paintings of monoliths, bazaars, shorelines and catacombs. Each run starts with your character accepting One Last Job from some dubious power-broker in the "Byzantine-flavored" Eternal City. Perhaps you'll be looking into the untimely deaths of some princelings, or maybe you'll be escorting a murderer: either way, you'll need to trek down to an underworld that borrows ideas from Ancient Greece and Mesopotamia.

The opening interview also defines your character, as you pick from backgrounds, strengths and faults. Ho thar! I am Caroline, seasoned sailor and scout, with the bestest biceps this side of the Hungry Sea. My major shortcoming: I like to make jokes about gods.

Having created yourself, you then recruit a crew of similarly imperfect adventurers, spending Question points to decide how much you know about them to begin with. A big hand for Sethre: diplomat, pickpocket and shaman, dream-dogged and impulsive. A round of applause for Hemze: catfooted spymaster, who looks like a bull's derriere. The characters you choose will form loose relationships, reacting to each other's traits as the yarn wears on. These relationships are strongly shaped by the task at hand, which might see you keeping secrets from your colleagues, or deciding in advance that somebody ain't coming back from the Great Below.

The heist itself consists of a series of round-based encounters drawn from a pack of over 280, each with a mix of solutions depending on your party's skillset. In a pleasing tactile device that makes me think yet again of Ursula K Le Guin, encounters are resolved using bags of tokens. Each round, you pull up to four tokens from three bags. You get one bag for the character you've selected to take charge of the encounter (which means you'll be able to play more of their tokens), and one for the rest of the group. A third bag houses tide-turning boons and knowledge you may have acquired by, say, befriending a sorrowful spirit, or jailbreaking a god.

The tokens mostly reflect each character's traits, both helpful and hindersome – "Nerinai is knowledgeable", "Chisu is greedy", "Sethre has a troubled past", "Esanth knows lockpicking". You apply these tokens to one of three actions, corresponding to the scenario. You're navigating the rapids of Styx: do you focus on the rocks, or on the unruly dead crowding the stern? You're helping the Fates weave your very own destiny: do you throw the shuttle, or offer to cut the warp threads?

Other, more generic tokens might grant you resources and buffs, or rid you of debuffs. Show Some Swagger will improve a character's morale, if played successfully, while Get The Measure earns you Insight points, which let you visualise the odds of each token being successful. Any tokens and actions not used up in a round carry over to the next, so you might want to reserve any tokens that could fit several possible actions. Conversely, you'll need to figure out when to dispose of tokens that seem bound to fail. "Hemze is ugly" probably does have a use at some stage – I dunno, maybe Narcissus is working a guard post somewhere, and you can invite him to give Hemze a makeover? - but I'm not sure it's going to help me rescue some drowning merchants.

You need to win a certain number of rounds, and avoid a certain number of losses, but fumbling the encounter doesn't end the game: you might incur an injury or receive a mood penalty, perhaps even lose a character, but you'll often achieve the story objective (like crossing a river) regardless. I've rarely felt the urge to reload a save, which isn't possible anyway.

While never a taut exercise in resource juggling, the encounter design does oblige a bit of strategy, thanks to some underlying combos and questions of timing. Some actions are best performed early, boosting your chances of doing something else – disarming traps before lunging for a treasure, for instance. Some are easier to do when you're ahead or behind on victory points. A few need to be reserved for the encounter's finale.

Sometimes you get a bunch of tokens that don't entirely fit any action, and must guess how the writers will play out the implications. So far, I've found those stabs in the dark more entertaining than jarring, but there have been a couple of moments when the storycraft felt somewhat meaningless, next to the invisible tallying of points. Over the course of the heist, you also need to think about gathering items that serve as quickfix solutions, sometimes allowing you to avoid an encounter.

As you'd expect from the whole "repeatedly going to hell" premise, the encounters can be pretty macabre. During my first run, I had to deal with some hags who can shave away character traits with a nasty look. During my second, I tackled a scenario for which a positive outcome would see a character being hung from a meathook.

There are plague crows, blade tsunamis, and mesmerising demons. Worst of all, there's a poetry contest. (I won the poetry contest, mostly by alternating between mockery of my opponent and flattery of the audience.) As grim as things may get, however, the writing remains brisk and buoyant, with characters squabbling a bit and maybe revealing something about themselves when they strike out, keeping up the momentum of the tale. I've come to love these little setbacks. It's like Scheherazade turning every tumble into a cliffhanger, with her head on the line. It's the kind of game in which a clean sweep feels like a loss, because you've bleached away the reversals and pratfalls that any thrilling adventure should involve.

Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists is out now on Steam. I reckon you should give 'er a go, especially if you enjoyed the art and writing of King of Dragon Pass and its spiritual successor, Six Ages, but found the village management element tedious. I should mention that the game's writers include Holly Nielsen, who has done stuff for RPS in the past.

items.title: TIFF 2026: 20 World Premieres We Can’t Wait to See This Year
items.author: Brian Tallerico
items.summary: It’s that time of year again! We’re back with a big team at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, which starts tomorrow with one of the biggest
items.text:
It’s that time of year again! We’re back with a big team at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, which starts tomorrow with one of the biggest programs in the festival’s history. Like every other year, TIFF is a mix of North American, International, Canadian, and World Premieres. It will give many people their first chance to see films from Cannes like “Fjord” and “Clarissa,” along with several Venice and Telluride options like “Wild Horse Nine” and “Ink.” While we plan to hit several films in Canada that other outlets have covered from Venice and Telluride (including highly anticipated titles like “Elsinore” and “Possible Love”), we always focus our annual preview on 20 movies playing nowhere but TIFF.

Come back for coverage of all 20 of these, plus about two dozen more, from yours truly, Marya E. Gates, Cortlyn Kelly, and Zachary Lee.

Note: All of the synopses below are from the official TIFF site.

“Babies”

Anchored by a pair of hugely appealing lead performances from Seth Rogen (TIFF ’25’s Good Fortune) and Oscar nominee Anna Kendrick (TIFF ’09’s Up In the Air), the second feature from writer-director Lauren Miller Rogen (Like Father) digs deep into the dilemma that comes for every couple: to parent or not to parent? Bolstered by an all-star ensemble that includes Issa Rae (TIFF ’23’s American Fiction), Dan Stevens (TIFF ’25’s Swiped), and Oscar nominees Sharon Stone (Casino) and David Strathairn (Good Night, and Good Luck), Babies is relatable, hilarious, and wise in equal measure.

“Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo”

A dizzyingly prolific auteur who never fails to imprint his signature on every project he undertakes, Japanese maestro Takashi Miike (TIFF ’01’s Ichi the Killer) returns to the Festival with this thrilling contribution to a one-of-a-kind cinema legacy. Like Abel Ferrara’s cult masterpiece Bad Lieutenant (TIFF ’92) and Werner Herzog’s gonzo Southern neo-noir Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call — New Orleans (TIFF ’09), Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo is very much its own entity, not so much a sequel to its predecessors as a mood, a variation on shared themes, and a rollercoaster ride through the darkest crevasses of the Tokyo underworld.

“Being Heumann”

Every bit as moving as her Best Picture Oscar winner, CODA, Siân Heder’s Being Heumann tells the remarkable true story of the woman who led a world-changing campaign for accessibility. Judy Heumann rallied a handful, then dozens, then hundreds of ordinary Americans with disabilities to push the US government to live up to its commitments.

The year is 1977. Raised in Brooklyn by German Jewish immigrants, and using a wheelchair since a childhood case of polio, Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) knows it takes grit and tenacity to get things done. So when Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo) refuses to sign meaningful regulations for Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the first national civil rights legislation designed to provide protections for people with disabilities, Judy devises a plan to force his hand, beginning with the occupation of a federal building in San Francisco, before going all the way to DC — and Califano’s front door — with a diverse team of self-described “radical crips,” creating solidarity through coalitions of marginalized groups.

“Closing Night”

Actor Cody Fern (American Horror Story, The Great Darkened Days, TIFF ’18) makes a sensational directorial debut with this sharp, emotionally astute story about family bonds and buried truths. When an internationally renowned movie star (Sarah Paulson) invites her estranged family to the opening night of her Broadway play after decades of silence, old wounds resurface almost as quickly as old habits. Her emotionally fragile sister (Naomi Watts, The Friend, TIFF ’24) remains determined to hold onto a lifetime of resentment, while her nephew (Toby Wallace, Finestkind, TIFF ’23) sees an opportunity to forge a relationship with his famous aunt.

“Diary of a Mad Old Man”

This captivating chamber drama from versatile auteur Wayne Wang (last at the Festival with 2019’s Coming Home Again) draws us into the troubled psyche of an aging widower whose sudden onset of disability coincides with the development of an unnervingly intimate relationship. Featuring a brilliantly graded performance by veteran actor Lily Franky (familiar to TIFF audiences from Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Shoplifters and Chie Hayakawa’s Renoir), this adaptation of revered Japanese author Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s eponymous novel ushers us into a realm of beguiling signals and unruly desire.

“Everybody Wants to F*ck Me”

Taron Egerton gives a gleefully committed performance as Adam in Jonathan Schey’s darkly comedic debut, riffing on the dating scene and the self-proclaimed “nice guys” who litter it. Adam has mastered all the trappings of enlightened masculinity: listening more than speaking in meetings with women coworkers, reading feminist literature, practicing yoga, and offering a soupçon of self-deprecation when chatting up women at bars or on dating apps. Adam’s longtime friend who once provided cover for his behaviour is growing up and growing weary of being an accomplice.

Adam has had a lifetime of f*ck around, but his find out is just around the corner when he meets Jessica Henwick’s Sofia. Intriguing and sharp, she proves to be a challenge calling out his behaviour. The encounter shakes Adam and, stranger still, everybody (but mostly women) start responding to his carefully studied charms, first with mild interest, then flat-out stalking, then vigorous pursuit — even when he’s appropriately dressed.

“Evil Genius”

Chilling, fascinating, and darkly hilarious, Courteney Cox’s second feature as director boldly dramatizes the bizarre web of stories behind the infamous “pizza bomber” incident. Featuring lived-in lead performances from David Harbour (Stranger Things) and Oscar winner Patricia Arquette (Boyhood), Evil Genius is an astonishing true-crime story brimming with bloodshed, betrayals, and a hopeless case of amour fou.

Erie, Pennsylvania, 2003. From a phone booth outside a waffle joint, Bill Rothstein (Harbour) calls the police to report the corpse of a murdered man stashed in a freezer in the garage of Bill’s former paramour, Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong (Arquette). But who is this murdered man? And exactly how did his body wind up in that freezer?

“Faith”

For single mother Gina (Erin Doherty, The Crown), every day is a balancing act. Raising her young son Jamie (Smylie Bradwell) while working shifts at a local factory, she does everything she can to build a comfortable home from modest means. When Gina meets the enigmatic and charming Michael (James McAvoy, California Schemin’, TIFF ’25) — a volunteer at the local food bank — his easy companionship offers the possibility of something she has long denied herself: the chance to envision a brighter future.

Then, in an instant, everything changes.

“God Bless You, Mr. Kopu”

“Unhappy? Need a change?” It’s a question, a sales pitch, and perhaps a warning. When charismatic American salesman Marco (Simon Rex, Red Rocket) arrives in New Zealand touting a revolutionary new cleaning product, he’s looking for ambitious recruits to build an army of door-to-door salespeople. Drawn in by Marco’s effortless charm and uncanny powers of persuasion, he quickly becomes his star protégé. But the story behind that box-office smash — which turned its unknown writer-star Sylvester Stallone into a phenomenon — is just as unlikely and inspiring. “The Julia Set”

For Julia (Chase Infiniti, One Battle After Another), mathematics has always come naturally. “Lemonade”

After years in Ireland’s foster care system, Danny is required by law to leave the home that has been his world. “Misty Green”

Superstar comic Chris Rock’s latest as writer-director is a hilarious, scathing satire of the institutional bigotry and soul-draining hustle that dominate the movie industry. “Onwards and Sideways”

With heartache, laughter, and hard-won connection, the latest from Oscar-nominated director John Madden (Shakespeare in Love, TIFF ’05’s Proof) stars Oscar nominee Laura Linney (TIFF ’08’s The Savages) and Rhys Ifans (TIFF ’23’s Mother Couch) as strangers whose lives become gradually entwined when both are diagnosed with Parkinson disease at the same clinic, on the same day.

“Prima Facie”

Anchored by a powerhouse performance from Cynthia Erivo, the Oscar-nominated star of Wicked and TIFF ’19’s Harriet, this piercing legal drama examines what happens when an ambitious barrister who primarily defends those accused of sex crimes unexpectedly becomes the accuser. Even when compared with his fellow mavericks, misfits, and adrenaline junkies who wowed audiences with their high-speed stunts during the 1970s golden age of daredevils, Ken Carter was one of a kind. What could go wrong? In short: everything.

It’s easy to see why he relies on steadfast allies like his wife Gloria (Laurence Leboeuf) and his car designer and technician Dick Keller (Ed Helms) — and why he’s so easily undermined by the machinations of his American nemesis, the legendary Evel Knievel (Ben Foster).

“A Talent for Murder”

This smouldering chamber thriller from director Anton Corbijn (TIFF ’07’s Control) imagines a strange confrontation between a literary agent and legendary author Patricia Highsmith, whose acclaimed, icily intelligent crime novels were the source material for such classic films as Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train and The Talented Mr. Ripley. Adapted by Joanna Murray-Smith from her play Switzerland and starring Alden Ehrenreich (TIFF ’23’s Fair Play), Olivia Cooke (TIFF ’19’s Sound of Metal; also at this year’s Festival in Slow Horses) and Oscar winner Helen Mirren, A Talent For Murder pits ruthless careerism against dark genius in a slippery battle of wills.

“Trash Mountain”

A dead hoarder’s houseful of holdings yields hope for a young man’s self-reckoning in this funny, wise film from director Kris Rey (It Was Great, But I Was Ready to Come Home). Featuring winsome performances from Caleb Hearon (The Devil Wears Prada 2), Zooey Deschanel (500 Days of Summer), and Oscar nominee Jackie Weaver (TIFF ’12’s Silver Linings Playbook), Trash Mountain is a homecoming story for anyone who dreads coming home.

“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother”

A showcase for the immense range and singular magnetism of Oscar winner Mahershala Ali (TIFF ’18 People’s Choice Award winner Green Book), the latest from writer-director Bassam Tariq (Mogul Mowgli) is an audaciously inventive Texas-set action thriller in which the line that separates religious devotion from righteous bloodshed evaporates in a cloud of mayhem.

Latif (Ali) is a devout Muslim and a loving family man who also happens to be a contract killer. He has a strict code: he never uses guns and he only accepts targets the world would be better off without.

We’re back with a big team at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival, which starts tomorrow with one of the biggest programs in the festival’s history. Like every other year, TIFF is a mix of North American, International, Canadian, and World Premieres.
